## The claim this tests

The [proposal](../../phd/index.qmd) is built on a council: many specialist models, each
covering a different dimension of market state, whose outputs are then reconciled. That
architecture has a prerequisite so basic it is easy to skip — **the specialists have to be
looking at different things.** If they all measure one quantity, their disagreement is
measurement error, and every downstream mechanism that trades on disagreement is
aggregating noise.

So before adding an eighth estimator, it is worth asking whether the seven already built
span more than one dimension.

## The check that looks sufficient and is not

The standard diagnostic is the **effective number of independent signals**, from the
dispersion of the correlation matrix's eigenvalues:

$$N_{\text{eff}} = \frac{\left(\sum_i \lambda_i\right)^2}{\sum_i \lambda_i^2}$$

It returns 1 when every signal is a copy of every other, and $M$ when they are orthogonal.
On the seven non-baseline estimators — `bocpd`, `cusum`, `ewma_slope`, `hmm_gaussian`,
`kalman_trend`, `ma_cross`, `ms_regression` — it returns:

| | NAS100 | US500 | US30 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| $N_{\text{eff}}$ of 7 | **3.84** | **3.78** | **3.82** |
| mean pairwise $\lvert\rho\rvert$ | 0.296 | 0.283 | 0.316 |

Roughly four independent dimensions out of seven, with low average correlation. I read that
as healthy and nearly stopped there. **That would have been the mistake.**

$N_{\text{eff}}$ cannot distinguish two situations that imply opposite next steps:

1. **Different dimensions.** Seven estimators genuinely measuring seven things decorrelate.
2. **One dimension, measured noisily.** Seven noisy estimates of the *same* quantity also
   decorrelate — because measurement error is independent even when the target is shared.
   Here a *higher* $N_{\text{eff}}$ means *worse* estimators.

Both produce a middling count and low correlation. The difference is not in the geometry of
the signals at all, so no amount of staring at the correlation matrix resolves it.

And the second reading is not a remote possibility. Simulate seven measurements of a single
shared signal, each carrying independent noise, and sweep the noise level: a
**noise-to-signal ratio of 1.29 reproduces $N_{\text{eff}} = 3.8$ exactly.** That is an
entirely ordinary amount of noise for a daily trend estimate. The observed number is
precisely what one dimension measured mediocrely looks like.

Two features of the correlation structure point the same way. `hmm_gaussian` and
`ms_regression` correlate **+0.934** — two Markov-switching Gaussian models that are very
nearly the same estimator counted twice. And `ewma_slope` and `kalman_trend` correlate
**−0.001**, which is *too* independent: two trend filters on the same price series should
agree somewhat, and a reading of zero suggests at least one is mostly noise being counted
as a dimension.

## The test that does distinguish

If the panel is one dimension plus noise, the information lives in what the estimators
**agree** on and the deviations are error. If the panel is genuinely multidimensional, the
deviations carry information too. That is a testable difference.

Each estimator's signal is standardised on a trailing window and split in two:

$$c_t = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M} z_{i,t} \qquad\qquad e_{i,t} = z_{i,t} - c_t$$

the **consensus** $c_t$ and each specialist's **deviation** $e_{i,t}$. Both are then scored
against the same volatility-only baseline, targets and purged walk-forward machinery used
in [RQ1](../state-decision-value/index.qmd), so the numbers are directly comparable to the
published decision-value work.

Three design choices carry the weight:

**Trailing-window standardisation, not full-sample.** A full-sample z-score leaks the future
into the scale of every signal, and it would inflate the apparent content of the consensus
— the exact quantity under test. The decomposition is asserted causal by recomputing it on
a truncated series and requiring a match to $10^{-12}$.

**An equal-weight mean, not a fitted first principal component.** A rolling PCA must
estimate $M$ loadings from a short window, and that estimation error would be attributed to
the consensus. An equal-weight mean has no estimated parameters, so it has no estimation
error to launder. This assumes the estimators load on the common factor with the same sign
— checked rather than assumed, and all 21 loadings are positive (0.41 to 0.83).

**One feature against one feature.** The headline comparison is the consensus (a single
feature) against *each* deviation (also a single feature), so neither side wins on feature
count. Throwing all seven deviations in at once is reported separately.

![Left: simulate seven measurements of one shared signal and raise the noise. Effective-n climbs from 1 toward 7, and passes through the observed 3.8 at a noise-to-signal ratio of 1.29 — so the count the real panel produces is exactly consistent with a single dimension measured mediocrely. Right: the test that separates the cases. Every point is a Diebold-Mariano t against a volatility-only baseline; negative means the feature improved the forecast. The consensus clears the deflated bar three times and all three are the volatility target. Not one of the 63 specialist-specific deviations clears it in either direction.](fig-specialist-redundancy.png){fig-alt="Two panels: effective-n versus measurement noise with the observed value marked, and t-statistics for consensus versus deviations against a deflated significance bar."}

## Results

Ninety comparisons in the grid, so the deflated bar is $\sqrt{2\ln 90}$ = **|t| > 3.00**.

**The agreement predicts.** The consensus clears the bar on 3 of its 9 comparisons — and
all three are the *volatility* target:

| consensus, t vs volatility-only | NAS100 | US500 | US30 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| direction | +1.90 | +1.29 | +1.36 |
| loss | +2.59 | −0.12 | −1.45 |
| volatility | **−5.52** | **−7.54** | **−4.54** |

On direction it is *worse* than volatility alone on all three assets. On loss it is a wash.
The one thing the seven estimators collectively know is something about future volatility.

**The disagreement predicts nothing.** Of the 63 specialist-specific deviations, **zero**
clear the bar. Only 13 reach even |t| > 2, in both directions, which is about what 63 draws
from noise would produce. The best is −2.48.

**And putting the deviations back makes the consensus worse.** This is the sharpest part of
the result. Adding all seven deviations alongside the consensus degrades it on every asset,
and on US30 it destroys the effect entirely:

| volatility target, t | NAS100 | US500 | US30 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| consensus alone | **−5.52** | **−7.54** | **−4.54** |
| consensus + all deviations | −3.62 | −2.83 | **+1.12** |
| deviations alone | +2.06 | +2.31 | +4.94 |

The deviations are not merely uninformative. They are costly — noise that a model has to
spend degrees of freedom fitting.

## What the consensus actually is

Two candidate explanations were tested and both fail, which matters because the surviving
one is much less flattering to the architecture.

**It is not agreement strength.** $\lvert c_t \rvert$ — large when the estimators agree
there is a strong trend in either direction — scores 1.32, 0.51 and 1.05 on volatility.
Nothing.

**It is not the council's uncertainty.** The cross-sectional dispersion of the estimators,
the natural "how much do the specialists disagree today" measure, scores 0.20, 0.17 and
−0.89. Nothing. This one is worth dwelling on: a council whose *confidence* was informative
would still justify the architecture even with redundant members. It is not.

**It is the leverage effect.** The *signed* consensus correlates −0.475, −0.491 and −0.498
with future 5-day realised volatility, and the tercile split is unambiguous:

| mean forward 5-day realised volatility | NAS100 | US500 | US30 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| consensus in its **bearish** third | **0.260** | **0.199** | **0.190** |
| middle third | 0.159 | 0.116 | 0.112 |
| consensus in its **bullish** third | 0.137 | 0.103 | 0.097 |

Roughly **double the forward volatility** when the seven estimators collectively lean
bearish. That is the well-documented asymmetry between returns and volatility, recovered by
an expensive route. Seven models, four apparent dimensions, and the entire contribution is
one signed number restating that markets get more volatile when they fall.

## The verdict

**One dimension plus noise.** The specialist tier as currently built does not span multiple
dimensions of market state. It measures direction, imperfectly, seven times.

This is not a small correction to the earlier reading — it inverts what to do next. If the
panel had four real dimensions, adding an eighth estimator would extend the council. Since
it has one, an eighth trend-family estimator would join the noise and *raise*
$N_{\text{eff}}$ while making the council worse, which is the failure mode this page exists
to name.

It also sharpens [RQ1's null](../state-decision-value/index.qmd). That experiment found
state estimates add nothing beyond a volatility-only benchmark across 168 comparisons. The
reason is now visible: the estimators were not nine views of the market, they were one view
held nine times, and the one thing that view knows — that falling markets are volatile —
the volatility benchmark already knew.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## What this does not show

This tests **these seven estimators**, on three equity indices, over 2015–2026. It is not a
claim that specialist councils are redundant in general, and a panel spanning volatility,
liquidity, cross-asset dependence and text would very plausibly answer differently. That is
the point: the gate is a check to run before trusting a council, not a universal verdict.

The result also rests on an equal-weight consensus. A fitted common factor might extract
more, though it would have to overcome the estimation error that motivated the equal-weight
choice.
:::

## What it changes

**For the proposal.** RQ5 asks whether explicit comparison of competing hypotheses beats
simple averaging. This is a *prerequisite* result rather than an answer: any mechanism that
exploits disagreement needs disagreement that carries information, and in this specialist
set there is none to exploit. Averaging is not merely as good as comparing here — it is
strictly better, because comparison would be reading noise. Testing RQ5 properly requires a
panel that passes this gate first.

**For the build order.** The next specialists have to measure something a single price
series structurally cannot express. Cross-asset co-movement, absorption, dispersion and
breadth are unavailable to every estimator tested here — not because they were overlooked,
but because they do not exist for one asset in isolation. A specialist reading those can
disagree with the trend consensus in a way an eighth trend filter never could.

**For the volatility benchmark.** The model that keeps beating every state description is
still a *benchmark* rather than a council member, and the consensus's only real skill turns
out to be predicting volatility. Those two facts sit awkwardly together and deserve their
own experiment.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Reproducing this

Everything here comes from `msl redundancy` in
[market-state-lab](https://github.com/davidolivermaguire-ai/market-state-lab):

```bash
msl redundancy --symbols NAS100 US500 US30
```

The decomposition's causality, and the demonstration that $N_{\text{eff}}$ rises with noise
on a single shared signal, are both asserted in `tests/test_redundancy.py` rather than
argued for here.
:::
